course: IB Mathematics: applications and interpretation HL

assessment.note: Standard AI HL external assessment (IA is the remaining 20%). Not from a file in the folder; check against the guide.

source_note:
* Sub-topic numbers and titles follow the IB Mathematics: applications and interpretation guide (first assessment 2021): SL 1.1–1.8,
  AHL 1.9–1.15, SL 2.1–2.6, AHL 2.7–2.10, SL 3.1–3.6, AHL 3.7–3.16, SL 4.1–4.11, AHL 4.12–4.19, SL 5.1–5.8, AHL 5.9–5.18.
  The guide PDF itself is NOT in `documents to process/MATHS`; the outline was transcribed for this app. Put the guide in
  `documents to process/MATHS/SYLLABUS/` to check wording. The five topics match the calculator book's master index ("BY IB SYLLABUS
  TOPIC", Topic 1–5 including Calculus), which is in the folder.
* Objectives, concepts, formulas, method steps, mistakes and recall prompts are study notes written for IB TEE (standard IB
  mathematics; formulas use the formula booklet's notation). They are not taken from the student's files and are labelled so in the app.
* Everything else the app shows (questions, markschemes, examiners reports, calculator sheets, worked solutions) comes from the files.

subtopics.title: Operations with numbers in the form a × 10^k
objectives: Write numbers in standard form a × 10^k, 1 ≤ a < 10, k ∈ ℤ
Calculate with numbers in this form, with and without technology
concepts: Standard form keeps one non-zero digit before the decimal point and moves the size into the power of 10.
Multiplying adds the powers; dividing subtracts them. Re-adjust a afterwards so that 1 ≤ a < 10.
The GDC shows standard form as 1.475E-1: you must rewrite it as 1.475 × 10⁻¹ in the exam.

formulas.name: Standard form
formulas.where: a: the significand, k: an integer power

method: Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is left of it.
Count the moves: left gives a positive k, right a negative k.
Check: 1 ≤ a < 10 and the value is unchanged.
mistakes: Writing 14.75 × 10⁻² (a is not between 1 and 10).
Copying the calculator's E notation as the final answer.
Rounding a when the question asks for the exact value.

recall.q: What range must a lie in?

subtopics.title: Arithmetic sequences and series
objectives: Use the formulae for the nth term and the sum of the first n terms
Use sigma notation for sums of arithmetic sequences
Model real situations (simple interest, regular increases) with arithmetic sequences
concepts: An arithmetic sequence goes up or down by the same amount d each step: it is a linear function of n.
The sum S_n averages the first and last term and multiplies by the number of terms.
Because n counts terms it must be a positive integer: round in the direction the context needs.

formulas.name: nth term
formulas.where: u₁ first term, d common difference, n term number

method: Identify u₁ and d (d = any term minus the previous one).
Decide: a term (u_n) or a total (S_n)?
Write the equation and solve for the unknown, by algebra or the GDC (table or solver).
If n is unknown, round to a whole number that fits the context.
mistakes: Using n instead of n − 1 in u_n.
Giving d the wrong sign when the sequence decreases.
Finding u_n when the question wants the total S_n (or the reverse).
Rounding n the wrong way (e.g. 66.7 boxes means at most 66).

recall.q: State the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence.
State the two forms of S_n for an arithmetic series.

subtopics.title: Geometric sequences and series
objectives: Use the formulae for the nth term and the sum of the first n terms of a geometric sequence
Use sigma notation
Apply to growth and decay (compound interest, population)
concepts: A geometric sequence multiplies by the same ratio r each step: it is an exponential function of n.
r > 1 grows, 0 < r < 1 decays, r < 0 alternates in sign.
A percentage increase of p% gives r = 1 + p/100; a decrease gives r = 1 − p/100.

formulas.name: nth term
formulas.where: u₁ first term, r common ratio

method: Find r by dividing a term by the previous one.
Choose u_n (a term) or S_n (a total).
Solve for n with the GDC (table, graph or solver) or logarithms.
Interpret n in context (which year, which month).
mistakes: Writing r = 0.05 for a 5% increase (it is 1.05).
Using rⁿ instead of rⁿ⁻¹ in u_n.
Off-by-one errors with years: u₁ is the start, so year 5 may be u₆ depending on the wording.

recall.q: State the nth term of a geometric sequence.
A value falls by 12% a year. What is r?
State the sum of the first n terms of a geometric series.

subtopics.title: Financial applications of geometric sequences and series
objectives: Calculate compound interest and depreciation
Use the GDC finance app (TVM) for interest problems
Include the effect of inflation and real value
concepts: Compound interest is a geometric sequence: each period the amount is multiplied by 1 + r/(100k).
Depreciation is the same formula with a negative rate.
In the TVM solver money paid out is negative and money received is positive: PV and FV have opposite signs.

formulas.name: Compound interest
formulas.where: PV present value, r% nominal annual rate, k compounding periods per year, n years

method: List what you know: PV, rate, compounding per year, years, payments.
Enter N, I%, PV, PMT, FV, P/Y, C/Y in the finance app; solve for the unknown.
Check signs and give money to 2 d.p. unless told otherwise.
For inflation, adjust the rate (real rate ≈ interest − inflation) or deflate the final value, as the question asks.
mistakes: Same sign for PV and FV in the finance app (it then reports an error or nonsense).
Wrong C/Y (monthly compounding is 12).
Rounding money to the nearest dollar when 2 d.p. are required.
Answering 23 years when 23.19 years means the amount is reached during year 24.

recall.q: In the TVM app, what must be true of the signs of PV and FV?
recall.a: They are opposite: one is paid, the other received.

recall.q: Which TVM variable holds the number of compounding periods per year?

subtopics.title: Laws of exponents with integer exponents; introduction to logarithms
objectives: Use the laws of exponents with integer exponents
Understand logarithms with base 10 and base e as the inverse of exponentials
Solve exponential equations with technology or logarithms
concepts: A logarithm answers: what power gives this number? log₁₀ 1000 = 3 because 10³ = 1000.
ln x is log base e, where e ≈ 2.718.
aˣ = b has solution x = log_a b; the GDC solver or a graph intersection also works.

formulas.name: Exponent laws
formulas.tex: a^m a^n = a^{m+n},\ \ \frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n},\ \ (a^m)^n = a^{mn},\ \ a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}

formulas.name: Definition of a logarithm
formulas.tex: a^x = b \iff x = \log_a b,\quad a>0,\ b>0,\ a \ne 1

method: Rewrite the equation as base^unknown = number.
Take logarithms of both sides, or use the GDC.
Check the answer by substituting.
mistakes: log(a + b) ≠ log a + log b.
Forgetting that logarithms are only defined for positive numbers.
(ab)ⁿ written as abⁿ.

subtopics.title: Approximation: decimal places, significant figures, bounds and percentage error
objectives: Round to decimal places and significant figures
Find upper and lower bounds of rounded values
Calculate percentage error and make estimates
concepts: Rounding introduces error; bounds are the smallest and largest values that round to the given number.
Percentage error compares the approximate value with the exact value, as a fraction of the exact value.
IB answers are exact or to 3 significant figures unless the question says otherwise.

formulas.name: Percentage error
formulas.where: v_A approximate value, v_E exact value

method: Identify the exact value and the approximate value.
Substitute into ε; the exact value goes in the denominator.
Keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer.
mistakes: Dividing by the approximate value instead of the exact one.
Rounding intermediate values and losing accuracy.
Giving 3 s.f. when 2 d.p. (money) or an integer (people) is needed.

recall.q: A length is 12 cm to the nearest cm. Give its bounds.

subtopics.title: Amortization and annuities using technology
objectives: Calculate loan repayments and the amount still owed
Calculate annuities (regular payments into or out of a fund)
Use the GDC finance app for all of these
concepts: A loan is repaid by equal payments; each payment covers the interest for the period and reduces the debt.
An annuity is a series of regular payments; the TVM solver handles both with PMT.
Total interest paid = total of all payments − amount borrowed.
method: Set P/Y and C/Y (monthly payments: P/Y = 12).
Enter the known values with correct signs (borrowed money is +PV, payments are −PMT).
Solve for the unknown (PMT, N, I% or FV).
For 'amount owing after n years', set N to the payments made so far and solve for FV.
mistakes: Mixing up P/Y and C/Y.
Giving PMT as a negative number in the final answer.
Forgetting the deposit/initial payment changes PV.

recall.q: What does a negative PMT mean in the finance app?
How do you find the total interest on a loan?
recall.a: Payments × number of payments − amount borrowed

recall.q: Which variable is the number of payments in the finance app?

subtopics.title: Systems of linear equations and polynomial equations using technology
objectives: Solve systems of linear equations in up to 3 unknowns with technology
Solve polynomial equations with technology
Set up equations from a context
concepts: A system has one solution when the equations are independent; the GDC equation solver finds it.
Polynomial equations of degree n have at most n real roots; read them all from the solver or graph.
Most of the marks are for forming the equations from the words.
method: Name the unknowns and write one equation per fact in the question.
Rearrange into the form the solver wants (ax + by + cz = d).
Solve with the GDC and check each solution against the context.
mistakes: Writing the equations in different variable orders.
Missing a root, or keeping a root that makes no sense in context.
Giving only the solver output without showing the equations (M marks lost).

recall.q: How many real roots can a cubic equation have?
What is the first step in a worded system problem?
recall.a: Define the unknowns and write one equation per piece of information

recall.q: Which GDC tool solves a 3 × 3 linear system?

subtopics.title: Laws of logarithms
objectives: Use the laws of logarithms to simplify and solve
Change the base of a logarithm
concepts: The laws of logs mirror the laws of exponents: multiplying numbers adds their logs.
Change of base lets the GDC evaluate any base using ln or log₁₀.

formulas.name: Laws of logarithms
formulas.tex: \log_a xy = \log_a x + \log_a y,\ \ \log_a \tfrac{x}{y} = \log_a x - \log_a y,\ \ \log_a x^m = m\log_a x

method: Collect logs on one side.
Combine them into a single log with the laws.
Remove the log by exponentiating; check that every log argument is positive.
mistakes: log(x + y) split into log x + log y.
Forgetting the power law when bringing down an exponent.
Keeping a solution that makes a log argument negative.

recall.q: Write log a + log b as a single logarithm.
State the change of base formula.
recall.a: log_b a = log_c a / log_c b

subtopics.title: Simplifying expressions with rational exponents
objectives: Simplify numerically and algebraically expressions with rational exponents
concepts: x^{1/n} is the nth root of x; x^{m/n} is the nth root of x to the power m.
method: Rewrite roots as powers.
Apply the exponent laws.
Rewrite in the form the question asks.
mistakes: Treating a^{1/2} as a/2.
Adding exponents when the bases differ.

subtopics.title: The sum of infinite geometric sequences
objectives: Find the sum to infinity of a convergent geometric series
State the condition for convergence
concepts: If |r| < 1 the terms shrink towards 0 and the partial sums approach a limit.
If |r| ≥ 1 there is no sum to infinity.
method: Find u₁ and r.
Check |r| < 1 and say so.
Substitute into S∞; interpret it (e.g. the total distance a ball ever travels).
mistakes: Using S∞ when |r| ≥ 1.
Forgetting to justify convergence when asked 'explain why the series has a sum'.

subtopics.title: Complex numbers in Cartesian form
objectives: Use i² = −1 and the form z = a + bi
Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers
Represent complex numbers on an Argand diagram
concepts: A complex number has a real part and an imaginary part; two complex numbers are equal only if both parts are equal.
Divide by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
The Argand diagram plots Re(z) across and Im(z) up.

formulas.name: Conjugate
formulas.tex: z^* = a - bi,\quad zz^* = a^2 + b^2

method: Expand brackets, replacing i² by −1.
Collect real and imaginary parts.
To find unknowns, equate real parts and imaginary parts separately.
mistakes: Losing the middle term when squaring (a + bi)².
Writing the imaginary part as bi instead of b.
Not equating real and imaginary parts to form two equations.

subtopics.title: Modulus–argument (polar) and exponential forms of complex numbers
objectives: Convert between Cartesian, polar and Euler forms
Multiply, divide and raise to powers in polar form
Add sinusoidal functions with the same frequency using complex numbers
concepts: Polar form describes z by its distance r from the origin and its angle θ.
Multiplying multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments; this makes powers easy.
Use radians for the argument unless the question works in degrees.

formulas.name: Modulus and argument
formulas.where: choose θ in the right quadrant

formulas.name: Products and powers
formulas.tex: z_1z_2 = r_1r_2 e^{i(\theta_1+\theta_2)},\quad z^n = r^n e^{in\theta}

method: Find r and θ (draw the point to get the quadrant).
Write the form asked for.
For products, quotients and powers work in polar form; convert back if asked.
mistakes: Wrong quadrant for θ from arctan.
Degree/radian mode mix-up on the GDC.
Not giving the argument in the requested interval.

recall.q: Write z = re^{iθ} in cos/sin form.
What happens to arguments when complex numbers multiply?

subtopics.title: Matrices: algebra, determinants, inverses and linear systems
objectives: Add, subtract and multiply matrices
Find determinants and inverses (2 × 2 by hand, larger by technology)
Solve systems of equations with matrices
concepts: Matrix multiplication needs columns of the first = rows of the second, and AB ≠ BA in general.
A has an inverse only if det A ≠ 0; then AX = B gives X = A⁻¹B (order matters).

formulas.name: 2 × 2 inverse
formulas.tex: A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix},\quad ad - bc \ne 0

method: Write the system as AX = B.
Check det A ≠ 0.
Compute X = A⁻¹B with the GDC and state each unknown.
mistakes: Writing X = BA⁻¹ instead of A⁻¹B.
Multiplying matrices of incompatible order.
Arithmetic slips in hand determinants.

recall.q: State det of (a b; c d).
When does a square matrix have no inverse?

subtopics.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalization
objectives: Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2 × 2 matrices
Diagonalize A = PDP⁻¹
Use diagonalization to find powers of a matrix and long-term behaviour
concepts: An eigenvector keeps its direction when multiplied by A; the eigenvalue is its scale factor.
With eigenvectors as the columns of P and eigenvalues on the diagonal of D, A = PDP⁻¹ and Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹.
For transition matrices one eigenvalue is 1; its eigenvector gives the steady state.
method: Solve det(A − λI) = 0 for λ.
For each λ, solve (A − λI)v = 0 for an eigenvector.
Build P and D in matching order; compute Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹.
mistakes: Columns of P in a different order from the eigenvalues in D.
Writing A = P⁻¹DP.
Taking the limit of Dⁿ wrongly when |λ| < 1 (it goes to 0).

recall.q: Which eigenvalue does every transition matrix have?

subtopics.title: Equations of straight lines; parallel and perpendicular lines
objectives: Use the forms y = mx + c, ax + by + d = 0 and y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Find gradients of parallel and perpendicular lines
concepts: The gradient is the change in y per unit change in x.
Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular gradients multiply to −1.

formulas.name: Line forms
formulas.tex: y = mx + c,\quad ax + by + d = 0,\quad y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)

method: Find the gradient.
Use a known point in y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Rearrange into the form the question asks (often ax + by + d = 0 with integers).
mistakes: Using the negative instead of the negative reciprocal for a perpendicular line.
Not giving integer coefficients when the form asks for them.

recall.q: A line has gradient 2/3. Gradient of a perpendicular line?

subtopics.title: Functions: domain, range, graph and inverse
objectives: Use function notation; find domain and range
Understand the inverse function as a reflection in y = x
concepts: A function gives exactly one output for each input in its domain.
The inverse undoes the function; its domain is the original range.

formulas.name: Inverse
formulas.tex: (f \circ f^{-1})(x) = x,\quad y = f(x) \iff x = f^{-1}(y)

method: Read domain from the context or the graph.
Find range from the graph (max, min, asymptotes).
For an inverse, swap x and y and rearrange.
mistakes: Giving the range in terms of x.
Forgetting restrictions from the context (time ≥ 0).

recall.q: What is the domain of the inverse function?
recall.a: The range of the original function

recall.q: How is the graph of f⁻¹ related to f?

subtopics.title: Graphs of functions; sketching with technology
objectives: Sketch graphs from the GDC with the key features labelled
Use an appropriate window and domain
concepts: A sketch shows shape and key points, not a plotted graph: label intercepts, turning points and asymptotes.
Use the GDC to find intersections between graphs to solve equations.
method: Graph on the GDC with a sensible window.
Copy the shape over the given domain.
Label key points with coordinates to the accuracy asked.
mistakes: Sketch outside the given domain.
Missing asymptote behaviour.
No labels on axes intercepts.

recall.a: Shape over the domain with key points labelled

recall.q: How do you solve f(x) = g(x) graphically?
recall.a: Find the x-coordinates of the intersections

recall.q: What does an open circle at an endpoint mean?

subtopics.title: Key features of graphs
objectives: Find maximum/minimum points, intercepts, symmetry, vertex, zeros and asymptotes with technology
concepts: Zeros are where the graph meets the x-axis; the y-intercept is f(0).
A quadratic's vertex lies on its axis of symmetry x = −b/(2a).
method: Graph the function.
Use G-Solv (ROOT, MAX, MIN, Y-ICEPT, INTSECT).
Write coordinates with correct accuracy.
mistakes: Giving a maximum value when the point (x, y) is asked.
Rounding coordinates too early.

recall.q: Axis of symmetry of y = ax² + bx + c?
What is a zero of a function?

subtopics.title: Modelling with functions (linear, quadratic, exponential, direct and inverse variation, cubic, sinusoidal)
objectives: Choose and use models
Find parameters from given information
Interpret parameters in context
concepts: Each model has a recognisable shape: constant rate (linear), symmetric turn (quadratic), constant ratio (exponential), y ∝ 1/x (inverse variation).
Parameters are found by substituting known points and solving.

formulas.name: Exponential model
formulas.tex: f(x) = ka^x + c,\quad f(x) = ke^{rx} + c

formulas.name: Sinusoidal model
formulas.where: amplitude |a|, period 2π/b (360°/b), principal axis y = d

method: Choose the model from the description or data shape.
Substitute points to form equations for the parameters.
Solve and interpret each parameter in context.
mistakes: Mixing up period and b in sinusoidal models.
Using the wrong units for time.
Forgetting the asymptote c in exponential models.

recall.q: State the period of y = a sin(bx) + d.
V varies inversely with t. Write the model.
What does d represent in a sin(b(x − c)) + d?

subtopics.title: Modelling skills
objectives: Use the modelling cycle: assume, build, test, reflect
Comment on the reasonableness and limitations of a model
concepts: A model is judged by how well it fits the data and whether its predictions make sense in context.
Extrapolating far beyond the data is unreliable.
method: State assumptions.
Fit the model.
Test against data; comment on fit and domain of validity.
mistakes: Generic comments ('the model is not accurate') without reference to the context or data.

recall.a: The model may not hold outside the data range

recall.q: Name one way to test a model.
recall.a: Compare predictions with data (e.g. residuals, R²)

recall.q: What should a limitation comment refer to?

subtopics.title: Composite functions and inverse functions
objectives: Form composite functions
Find inverse functions, including restricting domains
concepts: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): apply g first.
Only one-to-one functions have inverses; restrict the domain if needed.
method: Substitute the inner function into the outer.
For the inverse: y = f(x), swap x and y, rearrange.
State the domain of the inverse.
mistakes: Doing f first in f ∘ g.
Missing the domain of the inverse.

subtopics.title: Transformations of graphs
objectives: Apply translations, reflections and stretches, and composite transformations
concepts: Changes outside the function act vertically; changes inside act horizontally and 'the opposite way'.
method: Identify each change.
Apply in order (stretches/reflections before translations when building from the inside).
Check a point.
mistakes: f(x − 3) translated left instead of right.
f(2x) stretched by 2 instead of 1/2.

subtopics.title: Exponential, logarithmic, sinusoidal, logistic and piecewise models
objectives: Model with natural log, exponential (half-life), logistic and piecewise functions
Use regression on the GDC
concepts: Logistic growth starts exponential and levels off at the carrying capacity L.
Half-life: the time for a quantity to halve; k is negative in e^{kt} decay.
method: Recognise the shape.
Fit with regression or given points.
Interpret the parameters and long-term behaviour.
mistakes: Confusing L (the limit) with the initial value.
Not checking continuity at the joins of a piecewise model.

recall.q: How do you find a half-life from N = N₀e^{−kt}?
recall.a: Solve e^{−kt} = 1/2, so t = ln 2 / k

subtopics.title: Scaling with logarithms; linearizing data
objectives: Use log–log and semi-log graphs to linearize power and exponential data
Interpret gradient and intercept
concepts: If y = ab^x, ln y is linear in x (semi-log). If y = ax^n, ln y is linear in ln x (log–log).
The gradient of the linearized graph gives the exponent or growth constant.

formulas.name: Power linearized
formulas.tex: y = ax^n \Rightarrow \ln y = n\ln x + \ln a

method: Take logs of the data.
Fit a straight line.
Convert gradient and intercept back to the original parameters.
mistakes: Forgetting to exponentiate the intercept to get a.
Using the wrong axes (ln y vs x or ln x).

recall.q: Which graph is linear for y = axⁿ?
For y = ae^{kx}, what is the gradient of ln y against x?
Intercept of ln y against x is 2.3. Find a.

subtopics.title: 3D distance, midpoint, volume and surface area; angles in 3D
objectives: Find distance and midpoint in 3D
Find volume and surface area of right prisms, pyramids, cones, spheres and composites
Find angles between lines and planes
concepts: Find a right-angled triangle inside the solid for 3D angles.
Composite solids: add or subtract simple solids.

formulas.name: Cone and sphere
formulas.tex: V_{cone} = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h,\ \ A_{curved} = \pi r l,\ \ V_{sphere} = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3,\ \ A_{sphere} = 4\pi r^2

method: Sketch and label.
Identify the right triangle or the solids involved.
Apply the formula; watch units.
mistakes: Using the slant height as the vertical height.
Forgetting the base in surface area.
cm³ vs cm² units.

subtopics.title: Right-angled and non-right-angled trigonometry
objectives: Use sin, cos, tan; the sine rule; the cosine rule; area = ½ab sin C
concepts: Cosine rule: two sides and the included angle, or three sides. Sine rule: a side with its opposite angle.
The sine rule for an angle can have two answers (ambiguous case).

formulas.name: Cosine rule
formulas.tex: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C,\quad \cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}

method: Label sides opposite their angles.
Choose the rule from what is known.
Check the calculator is in degrees.
mistakes: Radian mode when the question uses degrees.
Using the cosine rule's angle not between the two sides.

recall.q: When do you use the sine rule?
recall.a: When a side and its opposite angle are known

recall.q: Area of a triangle using two sides and the included angle?

subtopics.title: Applications of trigonometry: elevation, depression, bearings
objectives: Solve problems with Pythagoras, angles of elevation and depression, bearings
Draw labelled diagrams
concepts: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, written with three figures.
Draw north lines at each point; alternate angles help.
method: Draw a clear labelled diagram.
Find the triangle and known angles.
Apply the right rule; give the bearing as three figures.
mistakes: Measuring a bearing from the wrong point.
Angle of depression placed inside the triangle at the wrong vertex.

recall.q: Angle of elevation is measured from?
Bearing of A from B is 070°. Bearing of B from A?

subtopics.title: Circles: arc length and sector area (degrees)
objectives: Find arc length and sector area with angles in degrees
concepts: An arc is the fraction θ/360 of the circumference; a sector is the same fraction of the area.
method: Find the angle and radius.
Apply the fraction.
For segments, subtract the triangle (½r² sin θ).
mistakes: Using the radian formula with degrees.
Forgetting to subtract the triangle for a segment.

subtopics.title: Equations of perpendicular bisectors
objectives: Find the perpendicular bisector of a line segment
concepts: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B (this builds Voronoi edges).
method: Find the midpoint of AB.
Find the gradient of AB and take the negative reciprocal.
Write the line through the midpoint.
mistakes: Using the gradient of AB itself.
Using an endpoint instead of the midpoint.

recall.q: What point does a perpendicular bisector pass through?
Gradient of AB is 4. Gradient of its perpendicular bisector?
Which property do points on it share?

subtopics.title: Voronoi diagrams
objectives: Construct and interpret Voronoi diagrams: sites, vertices, edges, cells
Add a site; nearest-neighbour interpolation; the toxic waste dump problem
concepts: Each cell holds the points closer to its site than to any other site; edges are perpendicular bisectors.
The toxic waste dump point is a Voronoi vertex (or a boundary point) farthest from its nearest sites.
method: Find perpendicular bisectors between neighbouring sites.
Keep only the parts nearer to those two sites.
Interpret: which site is nearest; best location.
mistakes: Drawing bisectors between sites that are not neighbours.
Forgetting boundary points in the toxic waste problem.

recall.q: What are the edges of a Voronoi diagram made of?

recall.a: All points closest to one site

recall.q: Where is the toxic waste dump located?
recall.a: At a vertex (or boundary point) farthest from the nearest sites

subtopics.title: Radian measure; arc length and sector area in radians
objectives: Convert between degrees and radians
Use arc length and sector area formulas in radians
concepts: π radians = 180°. In radians the formulas become simpler: l = rθ.
method: Check whether θ is in radians.
Apply l = rθ or A = ½r²θ.
Set the GDC to radians when trig functions are involved.
mistakes: Degree mode on the GDC.
Using the degree formula with radians.

subtopics.title: The unit circle; Pythagorean identity; trigonometric equations
objectives: Define sin and cos on the unit circle
Use cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 and tan θ = sin θ/cos θ
Solve trigonometric equations with technology in a given interval
concepts: On the unit circle, cos θ is the x-coordinate and sin θ the y-coordinate.
Trig equations have several solutions in an interval: find them all.
method: Graph both sides over the interval.
Find every intersection.
Give answers in the interval and units asked.
